vignette: Maria still remembers the feeling of being trapped in her childhood home, with no escape from the abuse that seemed to come at any moment. It's a sensation she's never shaken, and one that can still trigger an overwhelming sense of entrapment when she feels cornered or without options. When this happens, she finds herself instinctively seeking out safe spaces – always choosing where to sit based on how protected she feels, often with her back against a wall so she can see the room. This need for control has become second nature, but it's also left her feeling like she's constantly on edge, unable to fully relax. At night, Maria lies awake, vigilant and alert, listening for any sign of movement or danger. She knows it's irrational – she's safe now, in a loving relationship and working as a community organizer – but the memories of her childhood linger, refusing to be extinguished. Sometimes they come flooding back in vivid detail, like the time her caregiver... (she can't bear to think about it). Other times, they're shrouded in a fog that's just as unsettling. Maria tries to erase these memories from her mind, throwing herself into work or tasks to keep them at bay. But even as she buries herself in her job, the memories still seep through, manifesting in strange ways. She'll be leading a meeting or working with clients when suddenly an image will flash into her mind – a picture of her childhood home, or the look on her caregiver's face. It's disorienting and uncomfortable, like she's been dropped back into that moment without warning. For Maria, these memories are bittersweet. On one hand, they're all she has left of her past; on the other, they're a constant reminder of her own weakness and vulnerability. She can't shake the feeling that someone else would have stopped the abuse from happening – that if only she'd been stronger or more capable, things might have turned out differently. As a result, Maria often feels numb and disconnected from the world around her. She's built walls to protect herself from getting hurt again, but in doing so, she's also isolated herself from others. Her partner tries to be understanding, but Maria can't help feeling like they just don't get it – that no one truly understands what she went through. Lately, things have started to spiral out of control. Maria finds herself constantly checking behind her, afraid of being followed or ambushed. She knows it's irrational – she's safe now – but the memories and emotions still linger, driving her behavior. Her avoidance strategies are starting to take a toll on her relationships and work; her partner feels shut out, and her colleagues notice that she's distant and preoccupied. Despite all this, Maria is desperate to break free from the cycle of fear and self-doubt that has defined her life for so long. She knows it won't be easy – but with the right help and support, maybe she can learn to face her memories head-on, rather than constantly trying to erase them. Maybe she can find a way to heal, and finally start living the life she deserves.
